units.translation: 98-100a. Nor indeed the Bebryces: Apollonius indicates that Amycus had been killed; but Epicharmus (fr. 7 Kaibel) and Peisander (16 fr. 5 J.) say that Polydeuces bound him. Deiochus in the first book of his work On Cyzicus (fr. 9 M. II 19) says that he was beaten in boxing by Polydeuces. They did not neglect, he says, nor despise Amycus when he had fallen, but because of their barbarous nature they even stirred up war. 'Dry' (azēcheas) means the dry ones, those having a dry sound. The Cyprians call javelins 'sigynnoi'.
b. sigynnoi: javelins entirely of iron. Lg Gm Sm (P)
c. anti d' eascon: they went to meet Polydeuces face to face. Lg (P)

105-06. But he himself Itymonea: Polydeuces, leaping upon him with his heel, struck him. 'Lax' is the sound made by the toes of the foot. Or thus: properly the part under the toes of the foot is called 'lax'. Thus Posidonius (Bake 234) also interpreted it in the poet: 'striking with his heel' (Iliad 10.158).
110. Orides, son of Amycus: the penultimate syllable has the diphthong ei; thus Herodian in the third book of his General Prosody (I 67, 8 L.).

112-13. As far as the skin: up to the skin. 'Hoson' (as much as) instead of 'a little'. The iron passed through the very surface at the place just under the belt, but only on the skin, so as not to touch the internal organs.
b. He calls Iphitus 'menēdēios' (steadfast in battle) as being persistent in war; for 'dēis' is war and battle. P
115. azaleē: dry, since it is of wood. Homer also knows an iron one (Iliad 7.141): 'but with an iron club'. Some have interpreted 'iron' as 'well-strung', as also (Iliad 17.424): 'an iron din arose'.

116-18. Not yet to evil fate: not yet destined to die. Clytius was the son of Eurytus, brother of Iphitus. 'Dēōsesthai' means to be slain. Ancaeus is an Arcadian by birth, and he says that he was armed with an axe and a bear's hide. 'Thrasys' (bold) is used here in a good sense, not of recklessness.
119. tetagōn: having stretched out, having hurled. Lgr (P)
120. proschomenos: holding before him as a shield. Lg P

121. And together they rushed upon him: 'homou' (together) is used both of a gathering and of nearness, as the Athenians are accustomed to use it. Menander (fr. 851 K. III 227): 'the girl arrived at the very moment of giving birth' instead of 'near'.
